title: Sentence order
explanation: In English the verb sits in the middle: I drink coffee. In Korean it comes at the end: I coffee drink (저는 커피를 마셔요).
Small endings called particles are attached to words and show their role, so you only find out what happens at the end of the sentence. Listen for the verb.
The subject is often left out when it is clear from context. 커피를 마셔요 on its own already means 'I drink coffee'.
Time usually comes near the start, and the place comes just before the verb: 오늘 도서관에서 공부해요 (Today I study at the library).

examples.meaning: I am studying at the library today.

examples.note: No subject: it is clear who is talking.

practice.meaning: I study at the library today.

title: Saying what something is: 이에요 / 예요
explanation: 이에요 and 예요 mean 'is' or 'am' when you say what something or someone is: 학생이에요 (I am a student).
Use 이에요 after a noun that ends in a consonant (a batchim) and 예요 after a noun that ends in a vowel: 학생이에요, 의사예요.
Say the same sentence with a rising voice and it becomes a question: 학생이에요? (Are you a student?)
The negative is 아니에요, and the noun takes 이 or 가 before it: 선생님이 아니에요 (I am not a teacher).
In the formal 합니다 style both become 입니다: 학생입니다.

practice.why: 학생 ends in the consonant ㅇ, so 이에요.
우유 ends in a vowel, so 예요.
기숙사 ends in a vowel, so 예요.

title: Topic: 은 / 는
summary: Mark what you are talking about.
explanation: 은 and 는 mark the topic: what the sentence is about. 저는 means 'as for me' and starts many sentences.
Use 은 after a consonant and 는 after a vowel: 이름은, 저는.
은/는 also compares or contrasts two things: 고기는 먹어요 can mean 'Meat I do eat (unlike something else)'.
Once the topic is clear in a conversation, it is usually left out.

examples.meaning: I eat meat. I don't eat fish.

practice.why: 이름 ends in the consonant ㅁ, so 은.
저 ends in a vowel, so 는.

title: Subject: 이 / 가
summary: Mark who or what does something, or what exists.
explanation: 이 and 가 mark the subject: who or what does something, or what there is.
Use 이 after a consonant and 가 after a vowel: 시간이, 친구가.
은/는 sets the topic; 이/가 points at the new or important information. To answer 'who?', use 이/가: 누가 민수예요? 제가 민수예요. (Who is Minsu? I am Minsu.)
Two very common words change before 가: 저 becomes 제가 (I), and 누구 becomes 누가 (who).
Many everyday sentences use 이/가: 비가 와요 (it is raining), 배가 고파요 (I am hungry), 머리가 아파요 (my head hurts).

practice.why: 비 ends in a vowel, so 가.
시간 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so 이.
저 becomes 제 only before 가.

title: Object: 을 / 를
summary: Mark the thing an action is done to.
explanation: 을 and 를 mark the object: the thing that receives the action. 커피를 마셔요 (I drink coffee).
Use 을 after a consonant and 를 after a vowel: 밥을, 커피를.
In speech the object particle is often dropped: 커피 마셔요. Writing it out helps you learn it.
Some verbs take 을/를 where English uses a different structure: 친구를 만나요 (I meet a friend), 음악을 좋아해요 (I like music).

practice.why: 물 ends in the consonant ㄹ, so 을.
친구 ends in a vowel, so 를.

title: Place and time: 에 / 에서
summary: Where you go, where you are, where things happen, and when.
explanation: 에 marks a place you go to or are at: 학교에 가요 (I go to school), 집에 있어요 (I am at home).
에서 marks the place where an action happens: 도서관에서 공부해요 (I study at the library).
A rule of thumb: with 가요, 와요 and 있어요 use 에; with action verbs like 먹어요, 공부해요 and 일해요 use 에서.
에 also marks a time: 세 시에 (at three), 월요일에 (on Monday). The words 오늘, 내일, 어제 and 지금 never take 에.
에서 can also mean 'from' a place: 카자흐스탄에서 왔어요 (I came from Kazakhstan).

examples.meaning: I am in the dorm now.
I have a class at nine.
I am going to Busan on Saturday.

practice.why: Going to a place: 에.

practice.meaning: I drink coffee at a cafe.
practice.why: Drinking is an action that happens there: 에서.
A time takes 에.

practice.meaning: I read books at the library.
I have an exam on Friday.

title: Polite present: 아요 / 어요
summary: The everyday polite form of every verb.
explanation: Verbs in the dictionary end in 다: 가다 (to go), 먹다 (to eat). Take away 다 to get the stem: 가, 먹.
If the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아요: 살다 → 살아요, 좋다 → 좋아요. Otherwise add 어요: 먹다 → 먹어요, 읽다 → 읽어요.
Verbs ending in 하다 become 해요: 공부하다 → 공부해요.
When the stem ends in a vowel, the vowels merge: 가 + 아요 → 가요, 오 + 아요 → 와요, 마시 + 어요 → 마셔요, 배우 + 어요 → 배워요.
This one form means 'I do' and 'I am doing', and with a rising voice 'Do you…?'. It is the safe polite style for daily life.

practice.why: 가 + 아요 merge into 가요.
The vowel of 먹 is ㅓ, not ㅏ or ㅗ, so 어요.
하다 always becomes 해요.
마시 + 어요 merge into 마셔요.

title: Not and cannot: 안 / 못
summary: Say what you don't do, and what you can't do.
explanation: Put 안 before a verb to say 'not': 안 가요 (I am not going), 안 먹어요 (I don't eat it).
Put 못 before a verb to say 'cannot', when you would like to but are not able: 못 가요 (I can't go).
With 하다 verbs, 안 and 못 go just before 해요: 공부 안 해요 (I don't study), 운동 못 해요 (I can't exercise).
Adjectives take 안 too: 안 매워요 (it is not spicy). 못 is for actions.
Two words have their own opposite instead: 있어요 → 없어요 (there isn't), 알아요 → 몰라요 (I don't know).

examples.meaning: I am not going to school today.

practice.why: A plain 'not': 안.
'Cannot': 못.
The opposite of 있어요 is its own word, 없어요.

title: Past tense: 았어요 / 었어요
explanation: The past follows the same vowel rule as the present: 아요 becomes 았어요, 어요 becomes 었어요, and 해요 becomes 했어요.
So: 가요 → 갔어요 (went), 먹어요 → 먹었어요 (ate), 공부해요 → 공부했어요 (studied).
Merged vowels stay merged: 와요 → 왔어요, 마셔요 → 마셨어요, 배워요 → 배웠어요.
Nouns: 학생이었어요 after a consonant, 의사였어요 after a vowel.
Useful time words: 어제 (yesterday), 지난주 (last week), 주말에 (at the weekend).

examples.meaning: I went to Busan at the weekend.
This is my first time in Korea.

practice.why: 먹 has the vowel ㅓ, so 었어요.
하다 becomes 했어요.
오 + 았어요 merge into 왔어요.

title: Future and plans: (으)ㄹ 거예요
summary: Say what you are going to do.
pattern: Verb stem + ㄹ 거예요 / 을 거예요
explanation: To talk about plans and the future, add ㄹ 거예요 to a stem ending in a vowel and 을 거예요 to a stem ending in a consonant: 가다 → 갈 거예요, 먹다 → 먹을 거예요.
하다 verbs become 할 거예요: 공부할 거예요.
If the stem already ends in ㄹ, just add 거예요: 살다 → 살 거예요, 만들다 → 만들 거예요.
As a question it asks about someone's plans: 주말에 뭐 할 거예요? (What are you doing at the weekend?)
The present tense can also be used for the near future: 내일 가요 (I am going tomorrow).

examples.meaning: I am going to Busan tomorrow.
I am going to have bibimbap this evening.
What are you doing at the weekend?
I will study Korean next semester.
I am going to Korea in February.

practice.meaning: I am going to meet a friend tomorrow.
I am going to eat gimbap this evening.
What are you doing at the weekend?
I am going to Seoul next week.
practice.why: 가 ends in a vowel, so just ㄹ: 갈.

practice.meaning: I am going to read a book.
practice.why: 읽 ends in a consonant, so 을: 읽을.

practice.meaning: I am going to the library tomorrow.

title: Wanting: 고 싶어요
summary: Say what you want to do.
explanation: Add 고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do: 가다 → 가고 싶어요 (I want to go).
No vowel rules here: the stem stays as it is. 먹고 싶어요, 공부하고 싶어요.
Ask with a rising voice: 뭐 먹고 싶어요? (What do you want to eat?)
Past: 가고 싶었어요 (I wanted to go). Negative: 가고 싶지 않아요 (I don't want to go).
고 싶어요 is for actions. To ask for a thing in a shop or a cafe, use 주세요 (next lesson).
For someone else's wish, Korean says 고 싶어해요: 친구가 가고 싶어해요 (My friend wants to go).

examples.meaning: I want to go to Korea.
I want to make Korean friends.
What do you want to drink?

practice.why: 고 싶어요 goes straight after the stem 마시.

practice.meaning: I want to go to Busan.
I want to speak Korean well.
What do you want to eat?
I want to go to Korea.

title: Polite requests: 주세요
summary: Ask for things, and ask people to do things.
explanation: 주세요 means 'please give me'. Put it after a thing: 물 주세요 (Water, please). This one word gets you through cafes, shops and restaurants.
Add a number and a counter for how many: 아메리카노 두 잔 주세요 (Two americanos, please). Counters are in the Numbers deck.
After a verb, 주세요 asks someone to do something for you: 기다려 주세요 (Please wait), 도와주세요 (Please help me).
The verb takes its 해요 form without 요: 말해요 → 말해 주세요, 기다려요 → 기다려 주세요.
좀 (a little) makes a request softer, and people use it all the time: 물 좀 주세요.

practice.why: 기다려요 without 요 is 기다려.

title: Asking questions
explanation: A polite sentence becomes a question when your voice rises at the end: 학생이에요? (Are you a student?). In writing, add a question mark.
Question words: 뭐 (what), 누구 (who), 어디 (where), 언제 (when), 왜 (why), 어떻게 (how), 얼마 (how much), 몇 (how many).
The question word goes where the answer would be: 이름이 뭐예요? (What is your name?), 화장실이 어디예요? (Where is the restroom?)
몇 goes before a counter: 몇 시예요? (What time is it?), 몇 개예요? (How many?)
Answer with 네 (yes) or 아니요 (no).

examples.meaning: How do I get to the school?

title: There is, there is not: 있어요 / 없어요
summary: Having things, and where things are.
explanation: 있어요 means 'there is' or 'I have'; 없어요 means 'there is not' or 'I don't have'. The thing takes 이 or 가: 시간이 있어요 (I have time).
To say where something is, add the place with 에: 화장실은 2층에 있어요 (The restroom is on the second floor).
They are also your shopping question: 우유 있어요? (Do you have milk?) — 네, 있어요. / 아니요, 없어요.
Some common words are built on them: 맛있어요 (tasty), 맛없어요 (not tasty), 재미있어요 (fun), 재미없어요 (boring).
Past: 있었어요, 없었어요.

examples.meaning: The restroom is on the second floor.
Is there a convenience store near here?

practice.meaning: Is there a bank near here?
practice.why: 은행 ends in the consonant ㅇ, so 이.

practice.meaning: The restroom is on the first floor.
practice.why: Where something is: 에.

title: And, but, so
summary: 그리고, 하지만, 그래서, and the endings -고, -지만, -아서.
explanation: Three words join two sentences: 그리고 (and), 하지만 (but) and 그래서 (so). They start the second sentence.
그런데 also means 'but'. In conversation it often just moves to a new point, like 'by the way'.
You can also join two parts into one sentence with an ending on the first verb: -고 (and), -지만 (but), -아서 / -어서 (because, so). 비싸지만 맛있어요 (It is expensive but tasty).
-아서 / -어서 follows the same vowel rule as 아요 / 어요: 바빠서 (because I am busy), 피곤해서 (because I am tired).
The verb before -아서 / -어서 never takes the past tense: say 늦어서 죄송해요 (Sorry I'm late), not 늦었어서.

examples.meaning: I drank coffee. And then I studied.
It is expensive. But it is tasty.
It is raining. So I am staying at home.
This restaurant is cheap and good.
I am sorry I am late.

practice.meaning: It is expensive. But it is tasty.
I am hungry. So I am eating.
I ate. And I drank coffee.
I am sorry I am late.
practice.why: No past tense before -어서.

practice.meaning: This cafe is cheap and quiet.
It is raining, so I am at home.

title: Honorifics and the 합니다 style
summary: Speaking to professors, and formal situations.
explanation: Korean has speech levels. The 해요 style you have learned is polite and works almost everywhere. The 합니다 style is more formal: presentations, announcements, the news, and formal moments with professors or officials.
To form it, add ㅂ니다 after a stem ending in a vowel and 습니다 after a consonant: 가다 → 갑니다, 먹다 → 먹습니다, 하다 → 합니다. Questions end in ㅂ니까 / 습니까: 갑니까?
Nouns take 입니다: 학생입니다 (I am a student).
Honorific forms show respect to the person you talk to or about. Add 시 to the verb; in the 해요 style this gives 세요: 가세요, 하세요. 안녕하세요 is one of these.
A few verbs have their own respectful word: 먹다 → 드세요 (eat), 있다 → 계세요 (be somewhere), 자다 → 주무세요 (sleep). Use them for professors and older people, never about yourself.
Casual speech (반말) drops the polite endings. You will hear it between close friends, but wait until the other person suggests it before you use it.

examples.meaning: I am an exchange student at UNIST.
The professor is in the office.

practice.why: 반갑 ends in a consonant, so 습니다.

practice.meaning: I go to school every day. (formal)
practice.why: 가 ends in a vowel, so ㅂ니다.
For a professor, use the respectful word 드세요.

practice.meaning: The professor is in the office now.
